strengths: The manuscript is generally well written and organised. I liked that $(X=\mathbb{R}^2, G=\mathrm{SO}(2))$ was used through the manuscript as a running example.
The framework presented is fairly general and elegant.
Although I did not check the proof, the assumptions and results presented seem sound.
The framework is applied to several tasks, including in molecular conformation modelling and docking.
The authors use nice and informative figures (Fig 1 - Fig 3) to demonstrate the complicated geometric object related to Lie groups and have provided some level of intuition with them.
This paper has technically sound mathematical formulation and proof. The introduction of new SDEs based on Lie algbera is novel.
This paper provides numerical experiments on molecular conformer generation and molecular docking, which are important tasks related to structural biology.
While the paper may not be entirely novel, it is original, beneficial, and contributes positively to the community.

The paper does an excellent job of explaining how the new differential equation contains directional derivatives along Lie groups and why the directional derivatives to the group action have a Jacobian-like term, i.e., the fundamental vector field.
The paper is written in a way that is easy for others to understand. It is beneficial, interesting, and well-explained.
The interesting idea of using the infinitesimal generator of a group action to generate a vector field on the manifold is new to me.
The author claims that this approach enables us to design diffusion models on manifolds and handles non‑Abelian Lie groups as long as conditions in Sec. 2.2 are satisfied.
The numerical experiments are interesting since it seems the manifold structure is well‑learned in some synthetic examples. Applications on real datasets are also provided (MNIST and QM9).
I appreciate the rigor of the paper (with some caveats, see the Weaknesses section). Most of the quantities used in the paper are correctly introduced and I found the paper mostly easy to follow.
I think the proposed forward diffusion is interesting and worth studying.
I found the dynamics identified in Theorem 3.1 to be interesting. This is a nice link between some latent diffusion work and Riemannian geometry.
weaknesses: The framework feels pretty similar to building a generative model on the group $G$ (flow coordinates) itself using the reparameterisation $x(\tau)$ via the flow map; the reviewer questions the advantage of the presented approach over directly constructing a generative model on this space by mapping samples into the Lie algebra.

The presented formalism appears very similar to existing generative models without a global diffeomorphism (e.g., Corso et al. 2022, De Bortoli et al. 2022), raising the question of what advantage the current method provides for tasks such as Rotated MNIST and docking.
Theorem 3.1: The $\Pi$ term is akin to a covariance operator term right? (as in e.g. 'Score-based generative modeling through stochastic differential equations' Song et al 2021).

Line 273: 'specific order is irrelevant since the Lie algebra generators commute.' – how restrictive is this? Is this equivalent to assuming commutativity of the Lie group? E.g. does $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ satisfy this?
Line 281: Does this mean that one needs to go back and forth between the flow coordinates $\tau$ and the original $x$ at sampling time? Or only at the last iteration?
Line 291: How efficiently can one compute the flow map? I assume that the action itself is cheaper than computing the exponential map in general?

Section 5.3: Is the difference in energy differences significative here? What is the reasoning behind this group being beneficial? The reviewer suggests evaluating the samples via PoseCheck/PoseBuster instead of just looking at the Rdkit energy.

The paper does not provide a clear motivation on why and in what cases we should use this new class of SDE instead of standard Euclidean diffusion models; the lack of discussion makes it confusing when Lie‑induced generalized score matching is more beneficial.

The paper does not discuss how restrictive the technical assumptions are; feasibility of the three conditions in section 2.2 is not well discussed, and all examples are essentially Euclidean, raising doubts about applicability to more general manifolds.
The paper does not discuss the tractability of different score matching objectives in the general setting; it is unclear how the approach works when the data space is not Euclidean.
The numerical experiments are not performed enough and lack comparison with benchmarks in the literature, making it hard to assess the utility and advantage of the proposed approach.
Paper writing clarity can be improved; multiple typos and citations in inappropriate form decrease readability, and some figure captions are missing (e.g., Figure 5).
The explanations of essential concepts in the preliminary section are too similar to Wikipedia definitions, potentially lacking rigorous detail.
The presence of typos in the equations is another area for improvement; accuracy in mathematical expressions is crucial.
Uncertainty whether the framework can be applied when $X$ is a curved manifold; the reviewer asks for explicit discussion and demonstration on a curved $X$.
In Eq. 8 the order of multiplication of $O(\tau(t))$'s does not matter, which means the algorithm highly depends on Condition 3.

Assuming Condition 3, the reviewer derives that $[L_A, L_B]f=0 \rightarrow L_{[A, B]}f=0 \rightarrow [A, B]=0$, implying the Lie bracket vanishes on $X$ and suggesting $X$ is flat; they ask whether this is true or for a counterexample.
Lack of baseline experiments; the reviewer urges comparison with existing diffusion models on Euclidean data augmented with rotations and with Riemannian diffusion models for QM9 and CrossDocked2020.

Motivation and link with existing literature are insufficient; Theorem 3.1 is closely related to existing results on latent diffusion and prior work on diffusion models on Lie groups, which should be acknowledged.

Mathematical correctness: the paper needs clarification between the general data space $X$ and the Euclidean case; the definition of the key quantity $\Pi$ is poorly defined and its role in mapping vector fields is unclear.

Limitations are not discussed in enough depth; the procedure relies on access to the mapping $\Pi$, its inverse, and the ability to compute its determinant, which may be infeasible when $G$ and $X$ have different dimensionalities.
